Meta launched Muse. The agent books flights and pays. The rock band had their name taken away
On September 8th, Meta launched Muse - a personal agent that not only responds, but takes action: sends emails, schedules meetings, books tickets, fills out forms, shops, and can make payments. It works in the US, from 18 years old, in the iOS and Android app, on the muse.ai website, and on WhatsApp. Glasses are promised later.

There is a free tariff. Paid options are Power for $20 and Maximum for $100 per month. Meta's AI Chief Alexander Wang says: most people will be fine with the free version, the paid one covers the hardware bill.

The architecture consists of a separate cloud machine for each user, Secure VM with its own browser. Next to it is a second agent, Sentinel: it does not connect to Muse's network and services without its permission. According to the company, the agent does not see passwords and cards. It must ask for permission before sending an email or making a purchase. There are no ads inside, Meta claims that the dialogues don't go to Meta's ad systems. By default, chats can be used for training models - this can be turned off. Before the end of the year, they promise a Confidential VM, where the key belongs solely to the user.

The launch came two weeks after the multi-billion global Meta with its teams in social networks. Some employees complained about security flaws before the release. Bug bounties go up to $300 thousand.

Concurrently, another brand popped up. The British band Muse registered its name back in 1999. After the agent was launched, its handles on Instagram and X turned out to be linked to Meta's product.

The question is not whether the agent can buy a ticket. The question is - will you let Meta into your mail, calendar, and map.

🔐 Compliance Data Leak Exposes 291 Crypto Users' Identities

A data leak has linked the real identities of 291 crypto users directly to their wallet activity, stripping away the anonymity they relied on.

Copied support records exposed varying combinations of personal identity, location, and compliance data. Private keys and customer funds were not compromised in the incident.

The breach highlights a persistent vulnerability in crypto: while blockchain transactions can be pseudonymous, KYC and compliance records held by centralized services create a paper trail that, if exposed, can permanently de-anonymize users.

📌 Bitcoin price stalls near $82K as key resistance holds 

🌐 Bitcoin price pulled back after briefly breaking above $82,000 on Sept. 4, as traders took profits following a short squeeze driven by softer Federal Reserve expectations and renewed demand for US spot Bitcoin ETFs. According to data from cryptonews, Bitcoin price traded near $81,150 at the time of writing, having failed to hold an intraday move above the $82,000 psychological level. The pullback left the asset about 1% below its local high but still well above the $80,000 mark reclaimed during the previous session. 

⚠️ The rally accelerated after Bitcoin moved out of a range around $77,000–$79,000. Short sellers were forced to close leveraged positions as the price crossed $80,000, adding automatic buy orders to the market. CoinGlass data cited by market reports showed that the broader crypto market recorded more than $500 million in liquidations during the rally, with short positions accounting for most of the total. Bitcoin shorts reportedly absorbed about $415 million of those losses.

📊 Price action has since slowed near a technically important area. Galaxy Research data shared by analyst Quinten François placed Bitcoin’s 50-week moving average near $81,041, almost level with the current market price. According to François, Bitcoin has not closed a weekly candle above that moving average since November 2025. He said a move through $82,800 would also produce the first higher high of the broader downtrend and bring $90,000 back into consideration.

My acquaintance with conspiracy theories began shortly after 9/11. They made no sense to me because I knew the facts and had met people who were actually at the scene.

I was in New Jersey at the time and was in constant contact with a close friend who was receiving updates from the U.S. military.

On September 10, I stood atop the Empire State Building and watched the final sunset over the Twin Towers. Strangely, I remember asking my hosts whether those buildings were designed to collapse upon impact or topple sideways if struck by an aircraft.

The following morning, I watched the events unfold live as the second plane - United Airlines Flight 175, a Boeing 767 - struck the South Tower.

I know police officers who saw the wreckage recovered across Lower Manhattan, including a large section of landing gear, an engine, pieces of the fuselage, and other aircraft fragments. I also met flight attendants who lost many friends - and, in some cases, family members - who were aboard those planes.

Yet, to my shock and disbelief, I encountered respectable people, including pastors, who unashamedly claimed that no planes had ever struck the towers.

And what about Israel?

Although all 19 terrorists were identified as Muslims from Middle Eastern countries - 15 of them from Saudi Arabia - and despite Osama bin Laden, the leader of al-Qaeda, acknowledging and celebrating the success of the operation, people still pointed their fingers at Israel and claimed that 9/11 was a Mossad operation.

Therefore, the conspiracy theories surrounding October 7 - the claims that Israel initiated or orchestrated the attack - did not surprise me. I had already seen how this works in the aftermath of 9/11.

Conspiracy theorists do not allow facts to confuse them. They allow dark spirits to rule them.

🌐 Coldcard hacker uses THORChain to swap stolen BTC 

📣 A hacker associated with the third wave of Coldcard wallet thefts began converting stolen Bitcoin into Ether through THORChain on Sept. 3, according to Galaxy Research’s Alex Thorn. The transactions moved approximately 10% of the Bitcoin controlled by that attacker. Roughly 90% remained at its original addresses when he published the update. 

🔖 Researchers traced the swaps through THORChain to a newly identified Ethereum address. Thorn said he shared the address with law enforcement, crypto companies and other organizations monitoring the stolen assets. However, not every transaction succeeded. Thorn said the hacker appeared to be experiencing technical problems while attempting to process the swaps.

🔔 The cause of the refunds was not immediately confirmed. Possible explanations include liquidity limitations, transaction settings or protocol safeguards, but no verified technical assessment had established the reason. The movement represented the first detected onchain transfer from the original addresses associated with the first three attack waves, according to Thorn. Analysts will now monitor whether the resulting ETH moves to centralized exchanges, bridges or privacy services.
